subject: Dedicated vs Hyperscaler - capacity guarantees & next steps
messages:
From: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.inference>
To: Daniel Park <daniel.park@acme.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.inference>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.inference>
Date: 2026-10-12T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Post-call recap: Dedicated vs hyperscaler — capacity guarantees & next steps

Thanks again for the time today, Daniel — good conversation. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can align internally and get you a POC schedule.

Call highlights (short):
- ACME concerns: predictable capacity during peak product launches, cost control, and auditability for compliance.
- Hyperscaler approach: reserved instances + autoscaling, but you flagged uncertainty around guaranteed pre-warmed capacity and cross-tenant noisy-neighbor risk.
- Redwood Dedicated: reserved GPU pools + configurable burst policies, SLA-backed capacity reservations, and a private control plane option for stricter audit/KMS requirements.

How Redwood addresses the gaps you mentioned:
- Capacity guarantees: Dedicated provides committed slices (reserved nodes) with priority scheduling and a documented SLO for sustained throughput. We can include a provisioning guarantee in the SOW for the POC window.
- Bursting: We support controlled burst pools for short periods (configurable minutes/hours) with billing transparency — helps absorb traffic spikes without prepaying large flat reserves.
- Failover: cross-region routing + automatic fallback to a lower-cost compatible model variant if the reserved pool is saturated — reduces downtime risk.
- Observability & audit: token-level latency/cost breakdowns, model-level tracing, and audit logs that map to your SIEM.

Proposed mutual action plan (MAP):
1) Define POC goals: throughput (tokens/sec), p50/p95 latency targets, and peak concurrency number.
2) Redwood to provide: short one-week Dedicated POC offer with reserved nodes, onboarding guide, and a small SOW (attached).
3) ACME to provide: representative traffic patterns (sample traces), 2 engineers for integration, and procurement contact for SOW sign-off.
4) Schedule: kickoff next week — I propose Tue 2026-10-20 for a 60-min kickoff + environment provisioning.

Attachments: redwood-dedicated-vs-hyperscaler-brief.pdf (brief), acme-poc-sow-v1.docx (SOW draft).

Next steps: please confirm the POC goals above and whether the proposed kickoff date works. Happy to hop on a quick call tomorrow if you'd prefer.

Best,
Markus Klein

Thanks Markus — good notes. A few clarifying questions before we finalize the MAP: 

1) Pricing: for the one-week Dedicated POC, is pricing flat for the reserved nodes or usage-based with a minimum? Also curious how burst pool charges would appear on the bill.
2) Capacity SLA: can you sketch the language you typically use for a provisioning guarantee during a POC window? We need something we can show procurement.
3) Hyperscaler comparison: our infra lead is worried about long-term cost — how does Redwood's unit cost compare to buying committed capacity from our cloud provider? Any ballpark numbers or case studies?
4) Timing: Tue 10/20 should work for kickoff; can you send a calendar invite?

If you can answer 1–3 in writing we can loop procurement and get the SOW moving.

Appreciate it,
Daniel

Subject: Re: Post-call recap: Dedicated vs hyperscaler — capacity guarantees & next steps

Thanks — answers inline below.

1) Pricing for one-week POC: we typically offer a short Dedicated POC as a time-boxed commitment with a pro-rated flat fee (reserved node equivalent) to cover provisioned capacity + support. Burst usage during the POC is billed separately but we can cap burst spend for the POC and include that cap in the SOW so there are no surprises. For procurement, we can provide a simple fee schedule in the SOW (see attached acme-poc-sow-v1.docx).

2) Capacity SLA sketch (POC): "Redwood will provision N reserved nodes for the POC start date and maintain a minimum of X% of committed throughput for the POC period. If Redwood fails to provide the committed capacity for more than Y minutes cumulatively, ACME will be eligible for service credit equivalent to Z% of the POC fee." We can adapt X/Y/Z to ACME's tolerance; for the POC we typically draft a more developer-friendly, short-term SLA (examples included in SOW appendix).

3) Unit cost comparison: long-term unit cost depends on several factors (batching, KV cache hit rate, model quantization). In our experience, Dedicated with workload-aware batching and prefix caching can reduce per-token cost vs naively running equivalent reserved instances on hyperscalers by ~15–30% for steady inference workloads. Key drivers: our runtime optimizations, automatic batching, and ability to use quantized kernels where applicable. I attached a short brief with anonymized case studies and a costing model — this will help your finance/infra team run a quick apples-to-apples.

Calendar & kickoff: I'll send a calendar invite for Tue 2026-10-20 10:00 PT after you confirm.

Proposed immediate next steps:
- You: confirm POC goals and procurement contact.
- Us: finalize SOW with the capped burst number and SLA sketch, then issue DocuSign link.

If it's helpful, we can also run a short 1-hour technical deep-dive with your infra team prior to provisioning to align networking/KMS and tenancy boundaries.

Best,
Markus

Quick asks from my side before I send the DocuSign link:
- Can we offer a 10% introductory discount on the one-week POC fee if they sign within 3 business days? (helps procurement move faster)
- For the POC SLA, I suggested X=90% sustained throughput and Y=30 minutes cumulative outage; are those acceptable from an ops risk perspective?
- If not, what's the minimum we can guarantee and still feel comfortable (I want a short, defendable SLO we can meet without spinning dedicated capacity overnight).

I'll attach the SOW and send for signature once we agree. Also want to align on the internal owner for provisioning (who will own node allocation for the POC).
